claude.sample_unit: pregnant or postpartum participants who correctly recalled authorship (primary analytic sample)

links.outcome: Patient trust in content and physician when authorship disclosed as AI, physician, hybrid, or none
links.effect: AI-only authorship lowered trust in content (mean 9.43 vs 11.11; P=.001) and in the physician (8.93 vs 10.84; P=.03) versus physician-only; hybrid did not differ significantly (content P=.08; physician P>.99).
links.quote: AI authorship was associated with reduced trust in patient-facing education despite identical, clinician-written content.

links.outcome: Effect of labeling authorship (AI, hybrid, physician) on patient trust in identical content
links.effect: AI-only label reduced trust in content (9.43 vs 11.11; P=.001) and physician (8.93 vs 10.84; P=.03); hybrid label did not differ significantly from physician-only; engagement did not differ.
links.quote: AI authorship was associated with reduced trust in patient-facing education despite identical, clinician-written content.

links.outcome: Trust in content and recommending physician
links.effect: AI-only vs physician-only: content trust mean 9.43 vs 11.11, P=.001; physician trust 8.93 vs 10.84, P=.03; hybrid not significant.
links.quote: Among participants who correctly recalled authorship (n = 195), AI-only authorship was associated with lower trust in content (mean, 9.43 vs 11.11; P = .001) and the recommending physician (mean, 8.93 vs 10.84; P = .03) compared with physician-only authorship, while hybrid authorship did not differ significantly from physician-only authorship for either outcome (content: P = .08; physician: P > .99).
